newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNHCR seeks security pledges to return to E. Zaire.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR seeks security pledges to return to E. Zaire.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency said on Tuesday it was negotiating with Zaire's government and the rebels to obtain security guarantees for its staff to resume aid to about 370,000 Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire.
But spokesman Kris Janowski of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) reiterated that the best option for the Rwandan Hutus was to return voluntarily to their homeland.
"We think a return to Rwanda for most people is a better option than being stuck in the jungle without international aid," Janowski told a news briefing in Geneva.
"In the end it is probably a better solution for most people than staying where they are and being put through this never-ending odyssey," he said.
Some 170,000 Rwandan refugees reportedly fled Tingi-Tingi after the seizure of camps in the area, 230 km (145 miles) southeast of east Zaire's regional hub of Kisangani, by Zairean rebels on Friday.
Thousands were now on the road west to Kisangani, with the head of the 50-km (30 mile) long column about mid-way there, according to reports received at UNHCR.
U.N. aid agencies, including 12 UNHCR international staff, withdrew from Kisangani on Saturday because of security concerns.
"We are seeking security arrangements from all those concerned to allow humanitarian programmes to continue in eastern Zaire," Janowski said.

"The withdrawal from Kisangani, the logistics hub for our relief programme in east central Zaire, on Saturday was temporary and it is our intention to resume our work if the safety of our workers can be guaranteed," the spokesman added.

UNHCR was negotiating security guarantees from the Kinshasa government and rebels led by Laurent Kabila, whose forces are fighting to oust ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko. The rebels have captured a stretch of eastern Zaire bordering on Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Tanzania more than 1,000 km (600 miles) long since the start of their revolt in October.
The fighting has forced some 200,000 of an estimated 370,000 Rwandans to move from their camps at Tingi-Tingi, Shabunda and Amisi in eastern Zaire.
Another 150,000 to 170,000 Rwandans remain unaccounted for.
"Assuming Tingi-Tingi has fallen we have practically no access to refugees we had identified in December," spokesman Fernando del Mundo told Reuters.
Local Zairean authorities were trying to divert the column of refugees on the move toward the town of Ubundu, about 100 km (60 miles) south of Kisangani, according to Janowski.

"But our reports on the ground indicate that the refugees preferred to proceed to Kisangani," he said. "We are looking into facilities at Ubundu to plan for a possible emergency relief programme there if the refugees converge there."
The refugees include members of the Hutu militia and former Rwandan government army responsible for the 1994 Rwanda genocide of more than half a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates.

It was not clear if the refugees fled with the militia. The last time the rebels broke the stranglehold of militiamen over the refugees, when they overran camps in Goma region late last year, half a million Rwandan Hutus went home voluntarily.

If the malnourished refugees trek east towards home across rebel-controlled territory, it would take them a long time to reach Rwanda. If they head deeper west into the Zairean bush, aid officials fear many will die from starvation and disease.
On Monday, two UNHCR staff set out from Bukavu for Kingulube, some 140 kms (90 miles) to the west to set up an aid station for refugees emerging from the forest, Janowski said.
"We hope their presence there will prompt refugees to come out. We will help them to go back to Rwanda, if they wish to do so," he added.
